title: Danya Plays the BONGCLOUD!! | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: With the king already flushed out, the recovery plan is to castle by hand. The king doesn't have to hurry straight back — first complete development, then walk it to safety step by step.

Two routes present themselves: simply retreat the king toward e8, or fianchetto and shepherd the king to f8 by hand. The catch with the fianchetto is a pawn to b3 followed by the bishop swinging to a3 — that diagonal shot freezes the king in place and stops the manual castle.
So play g6 with a contingency in mind — meet b3 with the fianchetto, and if the bishop lunges to a3, just drop the king back to e8. Every setup has its own answer.
The rook goes to e8, not f8 — putting it on f8 would jam the king's own escape route. With the file cleared, the king can march to f8 and onward to g8, and the by-hand castle is done.

All those tempi spent, it's time to hit back in the centre. The opponent's kingside build-up looks imposing but it's flimsy — leave it untouched and it becomes total positional domination, so it has to be challenged.

The pawn storm looks scary but isn't — the setup is rock-solid, and if the h-pawn captures on g6 it's simply recaptured with no damage. Understanding that the structure holds is what lets the counterplay proceed calmly.

Here's the counter-intuitive call: yes, capture again on c4. Most of the time the cautious answer would be to hold off, but not here — it saddles the opponent with an isolated queen's pawn on d4, and the queen immediately leans on it. Opening the centre also pulls the opponent's focus away from the kingside attack. Best of all worlds.

Now bring out the last knight. One plan is the slow route — reroute it toward the blockade square in front of the isolated pawn. The more direct plan is to send it to c6 and trade off the opponent's strong advanced knight as fast as possible.

To prepare the fianchetto with b6, the knight it leaves loose has to be defended first — and not by a bishop, which would defeat the whole point of the long diagonal. The queen is the defender, but from a square that keeps the pressure on the isolated pawn: that's why d6 is right and c7 or b6 are not.

The queen slides across to guard against the b6 break, since the fianchetto would run into a capture and a pin winning the exchange. The reply is to jab the queen with the knight to b4, chasing it off so that b6 becomes playable after all. Be stubborn with a sound idea — remove the obstacle rather than abandon the plan.

Rather than blunder the rook to the immediate break, prepare it with a rook to b8, and then the pawn can even come with tempo. And a deeper point: leave the isolated pawn alive rather than snatching it. Grabbing it flings the centre open, and in a cramped position an open centre favours the better-developed side — keeping the file closed keeps the pressure off.
So instead of the passive push, play b5 — the same fianchetto idea but with a tempo attached, hitting a piece on the way.

That advanced enemy knight is nothing to fear — the moment it's challenged, the reply is to drop a knight back to d5, the ideal blockading square right in front of the isolated pawn. From there, just keep making active moves; positions like this have no formula, only piece improvement.

The method is exactly that — scan for the piece that can be improved. A knight can spring forward to e4; a rook belongs where it shields the vulnerable e-pawn and discourages sacrifices on f7. Don't hunt for an algorithm; look around and upgrade your worst-placed piece.
The queen's advance left the bishop undefended — and that changes the maths. Now a retreat to d5 is enticing precisely because it hits that loose bishop.

Recapture with the queen to start building a battery. It seems to abandon the defence of a key square, but this is the long game — if the opposing queen ever shifts, the battery is already loaded. There's no downside to preparing for the future.

A tool for scary-looking threats — the best-and-worst-case test. If unsure whether the opponent's plan is dangerous, imagine letting them carry it out in full and ask how bad the result really is. Here even a queen landing next to the king is met with a quiet king step, and it amounts to nothing.
Infiltrate with the rook to c2, and now notice the enemy queen is overloaded — it's guarding two things at once and can't hold both. The knight jump to f6 is the threat that exploits the overload.
The knight lunge that grabs a pawn is desperation — so don't reflexively recapture. The far stronger continuation keeps the overload theme alive rather than snatching the offered piece.
The cleanest kill is the rook crashing in with check — that was the whole idea. If the queen takes, it's mate; the material is already decisive, so there's no need to be distracted by side pawns.

When both queens are hanging at once, the first thing to look for is whether your own queen can escape with check — buying the tempo to survive. Here the check on c4 does exactly that and wins the queen.

Every version of this exposed-king structure has its own antidote. Against the plain version the recipe is to rip the centre open as fast as possible, and the whole fight boils down to whether the by-hand castle can be completed — the pawn-to-b3-and-bishop-to-a3 idea being the way to stop it.
